summary: An informational summary of techniques for repairing continuous media streams, like audio and video, that lose packets in transit.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2354 is a survey of ways to repair an audio or video stream after the network loses part of it. It compares four techniques and explains when each one is worth its cost.

subtitle: A survey of ways a sender can protect audio and video streams from lost packets.

tldr.problem: Audio and video streams sent with RTP over UDP lose packets, and each lost packet damages the quality of what the receiver plays.
tldr.mechanism: The memo summarizes four sender-side repair techniques, retransmission, media-independent forward error correction, media-specific forward error correction and interleaving, and says which suit interactive and non-interactive use.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational introduction, not a standard. It recommends low-latency forward error correction for interactive sessions and warns that repair traffic must not make congestion worse.

today: RFC 2354 is an Informational memo from June 1998, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself notes that it was written before any standard congestion control existed for streamed media.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Repair
sections.content:
A number of applications use RTP over UDP to deliver continuous media streams. Because UDP delivery is unreliable, the quality of the received stream is adversely affected by packet loss. A number of techniques exist by which the effects of packet loss may be repaired, and they have a wide range of applicability and require varying degrees of protocol support. The memo discusses a number of them and makes recommendations for their applicability.

The document says at the outset that it is introductory in nature and does not attempt to be comprehensive. In particular, it restricts the discussion to repair techniques which require the involvement of the sender of a media stream, and does not discuss the possibilities for receiver-based repair. For a more detailed survey, the reader is directed to a survey paper by Carle and Biersack.
sections.plainLanguage: Streaming media is sent over UDP, which makes no promises about delivery, so some packets arrive missing. This memo looks at what the sender can do about that.

sections.title: Units, Packets and Interactive Sessions
sections.content:
A unit is a timed interval of media data, typically derived from the workings of the media coder. A packet comprises one or more units, encapsulated for transmission over the network. For example, many audio coders operate on 20ms units, which are typically combined to produce 40ms or 80ms packets for transmission.

The framework of RTP is assumed, which means packets have a sequence number and a timestamp. The sequence number denotes the order in which packets are transmitted and is used to detect losses, and the timestamp determines the playout order of units. Most loss recovery schemes rely on units being sent out of order, so an application must use the RTP timestamp to schedule playout.

The use of RTP allows several different media coders to be used, with a payload type field distinguishing between them at the receiver. Some loss repair schemes send multiple copies of units, at different times and possibly with different encodings, to increase the probability that a receiver has something to decode. The receiver is assumed to have a quality ranking of the differing encodings and so is capable of choosing the best unit for playout given multiple options.

A session is defined as interactive if the end-to-end delay is less than 250ms, including media coding and decoding, network transit and host buffering.
sections.plainLanguage: Two time scales matter here: the piece of media the coder produces, and the packet that carries it. A session counts as interactive when the whole round trip, from encoding to playback, stays under a quarter of a second.

sections.title: How Packets Are Lost
sections.content:
Studies of the loss characteristics of the Mbone give broadly similar results: in a large conference it is inevitable that some receivers will experience packet loss. Packet traces taken by Handley show a session in which most receivers experience loss in the range 2 to 5 percent, with a somewhat smaller number seeing significantly higher loss rates.

It has also been shown that the vast majority of losses are of single packets. Burst losses of two or more packets are around an order of magnitude less frequent than single packet loss, although they do occur more often than would be expected from a purely random process. Longer burst losses, of the order of tens of packets, occur infrequently. The report reads these results as consistent with a network where small amounts of transient congestion cause the majority of packet loss, and notes that in a few cases a network link is found to be severely overloaded, and large amounts of loss result.

The consequence for a repair scheme is that its primary focus must be to correct single packet loss, since that is by far the most frequent occurrence. It is desirable that losses of a relatively small number of consecutive packets may also be repaired, since such losses represent a small but noticeable fraction of observed losses, while the correction of large bursts of loss is of considerably less importance.
sections.plainLanguage: In a big conference, most listeners lose a few percent of the packets, and nearly all the loss comes as single missing packets rather than runs of them. So a repair method should aim at the single missing packet.

sections.title: The Four Repair Techniques
sections.content:
Retransmission is the obvious way to repair loss. It is of value in non-interactive applications with relaxed delay bounds, but the delay it imposes means it does not typically perform well for interactive use. There is also a potentially large bandwidth overhead: not only are units of data sent multiple times, but additional control traffic must flow to request the retransmission. In a large Mbone session most packets are lost by at least one receiver, so asking for most of them to be retransmitted may cost more than the use of forward error correction. That leads to a natural synergy between the two mechanisms, with a forward error correction scheme repairing all single packet losses and those receivers experiencing burst losses, and willing to accept the extra latency, using retransmission as an additional recovery mechanism. The retransmitted units may be piggy-backed onto the ongoing transmission, which also allows them to be recoded in a different format to reduce bandwidth further, and FEC information may be sent in response to retransmission requests so that a single retransmission can repair several losses.

Forward error correction adds repair data to a media stream so that the receiver can repair loss with no further reference to the sender. There are two classes of repair data: those independent of the contents of the stream, and those that use knowledge of the stream. Media-independent FEC adds redundant data in separate packets, calculated with the mathematics of finite fields. The simplest is GF(2), where addition is just the exclusive-or operation, and basic schemes transmit k data packets with n-k parity packets, allowing the original data to be reconstructed from any k of the n transmitted packets. The advantage of parity-based FEC is that it is media independent and gives exact repair of lost packets, with relatively light processing, while the disadvantage is higher latency than the media-specific schemes. Codes based on higher-order finite fields, such as Reed-Solomon codes, are more sophisticated and computationally demanding, are usually structured for good burst loss protection, and typically come at the expense of increased latency.

Media-specific FEC uses knowledge of the media compression scheme to repair a stream more efficiently. If the units of media data are packets, or several units fit in a packet, it is logical to use the unit as the level of redundancy and send duplicate units, recoding the redundant copy to make significant bandwidth savings at the cost of extra computation and approximate repair. If media units span multiple packets, as with video, it is sensible to include redundancy directly in the output of the codec; the proposed RTP payload for H.263+ includes multiple copies of key portions of the stream, separated to avoid the problems of packet loss, which is efficient because the codec designer knows exactly which parts of the stream matter most and is of low complexity since each unit is coded once only. A third option is to apply media-independent FEC to the most significant bits of a codec's output rather than over the whole packet, which has low computational cost and can be tailored to represent an arbitrary fraction of the transmitted data. The advantage of media-specific FEC is low latency, with only a single-packet delay added, which makes it suitable for interactive applications.

Interleaving is useful when the unit size is smaller than the packet size and end-to-end delay is unimportant. Units are resequenced before transmission so that originally adjacent units are separated by a guaranteed distance in the transmitted stream, and are returned to their original order at the receiver. If units are 5ms long and packets are 20ms, that is four units per packet, the first packet could contain units 1, 5, 9 and 13, the second units 2, 6, 10 and 14, and so on. The loss of a single packet then produces several small gaps in the reconstructed stream instead of one large gap. The size of the gaps depends on the degree of interleaving and can be made arbitrarily small at the expense of additional latency. The obvious disadvantage of interleaving is that it increases latency, but the major advantage is that it does not increase the bandwidth requirements of a stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Four answers: ask for the missing piece again, ship extra data that can rebuild it, ship a second copy made by the coder, or spread the data out so a loss hurts less. Each costs something different: time, bandwidth, or effort.

sections.title: Recommendations and Congestion
sections.content:
For a non-interactive one-way transmission in the style of a radio or television broadcast, latency matters much less than reception quality, and interleaving, retransmission or FEC are all appropriate. If approximate repair is acceptable, interleaving is clearly to be preferred, because it does not increase the bandwidth of a stream. Media-independent FEC is typically the next best option, since a single FEC packet can repair several lost packets.

In an interactive session the delay imposed by interleaving and retransmission is not acceptable, and a low-latency FEC scheme is the only suitable means of repair. The choice between media-independent and media-specific forward error correction is less clear-cut: media-specific FEC can be made more efficient but requires modification to the output of the codec, so when defining the packet format for a new codec it is the appropriate technique and should be encouraged. If an existing codec is to be used, a media-independent scheme is usually easier to implement and can perform well, and such a stream may be augmented with retransmission for receivers willing to tolerate the delay.

The memo warns that adding large amounts of repair data when loss is detected will increase network congestion, and hence packet loss, worsening the problem that the error correction was meant to solve. At the time of writing there was no standard solution to congestion control for streamed media, though a number of contributions showed the likely form the solution would take, typically some form of layered encoding over multiple channels with receivers joining and leaving layers in response to packet loss, aiming to emulate the congestion control behaviour of TCP and compete fairly with non-real-time traffic.

As a guide to reasonable behaviour, the memo uses the relation between the loss rate and the throughput of a TCP connection, T = (s * c) / (RTT * sqrt(p)), where T is the observed throughput in octets per second, s the packet size in octets, RTT the round-trip time in seconds, p the packet loss rate, and c a constant in the range 0.9 to 1.5, with 1.22 suggested. Using this, one may determine the packet loss rate that would result in a given throughput if a TCP connection were used, which also gives an estimate of the acceptable loss rate for a streaming application using the same path that wants to coexist fairly with TCP traffic. The memo works an example: an RTP audio session with DVI encoding and 40ms data packets has a 40 byte RTP/UDP/IP header, 4 bytes of codec state and 160 bytes of media data, giving a packet size of 204 bytes, and sends 25 packets per second, giving T = 4800. With a round-trip time of 200ms estimated from RTCP reception report statistics, the reasonable packet loss rate works out at 6.7 percent, which would be an upper bound on the loss the application should be designed to tolerate. The memo notes that such a round-trip time estimate is at best approximate, and that for a multicast group it can only be an average measure.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-way broadcast can afford to wait, so spreading the data out is cheapest. A live conversation cannot, so the extra data has to be small and sent along with the original. And whatever the method, sending extra repair data when the network is already congested makes things worse, so there has to be a limit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Some of the repair techniques discussed in the document result in the transmission of additional traffic to correct for the effects of packet loss. Application designers should be aware that the transmission of large amounts of repair traffic will increase network congestion, and hence packet loss, leading to a worsening of the problem that the use of error correction was intended to solve. At its worst, the memo says, this can lead to excessive network congestion and may constitute a denial of service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Repair data is extra traffic. If a sender responds to loss by flooding the network, it can turn a small problem into a large one, and that could be used as an attack.

items.title: Broadcast, approximate repair acceptable
items.text: Interleaving, because it does not increase the bandwidth of the stream.

items.title: Broadcast, exact repair wanted
items.text: Media-independent FEC, since one FEC packet can repair several losses.

items.title: Interactive session
items.text: A low-latency FEC scheme; interleaving and retransmission add too much delay.

items.title: A new codec
items.text: Media-specific FEC, since the coder knows which parts of the stream matter most.

items.title: An existing codec
items.text: Media-independent FEC, which is easier to implement and can perform well.

items.title: Always
items.text: Repair traffic must not add to congestion, or it makes the loss worse.
